Figure 6b: Drying Rate and Sample Temperature vs. Dry Basis Moisture Content for a 300 GSM Softwood Bleached Trial The instantaneous drying rates, sample temperature, and moisture content were then used to compute sample absorbed energies, heat, and mass transfer coefficients. The transfer coefficients are represented as a function of moisture content to study its dependence on sample moisture and thereby deduce a correlation. The instantaneous heat transfer coefficients normalized with the initial heat transfer coefficients calculated as a function of moisture content are represented by Figures 7. Contact (Conduction) heat transfer coefficients are significantly higher in magnitude than convection heat transfer coefficients. Individual depiction and analysis of conduction and convection heat transfer coefficients help to deduce more meaningful conclusions and correlations primarily due to the differences in magnitudes. The trend observed in both contact and convection (non-contact) heat transfer coefficients is similar, with higher transfer coefficients in the constant rate zone (higher moisture) and a declining trend as the sample gets drier. Another observation was that the convection coefficients have a higher presence of noise in the data. This can be attributed to the flow disturbances and the effect of the hot plates during the interchange of contact to non-contact operation. 16 DE-EE0009395 Figure 7: Normalized Conduction and Convection Heat Transfer Coefficient and Mass Transfer Coefficient vs. Normalized Dry Basis Moisture Content for a 300 GSM Softwood Bleached Trial Similar to the heat transfer coefficient calculations, the convective mass transfer coefficients normalized with the initial mass transfer coefficient calculated as a function of moisture content for the trial can also be observed in Figure 7. The mass transfer coefficients were calculated in real-time using the water vapor concentration measured by the laser at the inlet and outlet of the chamber, drying rates, and the computed water vapor concentration in the sample using the Goff- Gratch equation and the temperature of the sample measured by the thermocouples. These mass transfer coefficients were calculated using the water vapor concentration gradient between the convective air and the moisture of the sample. Similar to the drying rate curve and heat transfer coefficients, it can be seen that the mass transfer coefficient is high at the beginning of the test when the sample has higher moisture content and has a decreasing trend as the falling rate period occurs and the sample is dried. Even though the inlet air temperature and flow rate were kept constant during the experiment, the fluctuations in the instantaneous mass transfer coefficient can be attributed to drying rate variations due to the heating and cooling cycles and the dilution and mixing.
